title: Prasidh Krishna Had Not Played a Test in India for Three Years. On Sunday, He Reminded Everyone Why He Should.
excerpt: The Karnataka quick dismissed both Atal and Shahidi to break Afghanistan's resistance in Mullanpur, bowling with the kind of control and hostility that had gone missing since his debut series.
body:
When Prasidh Krishna bowled Sediqullah Atal with a delivery that straightened viciously off the seam on Sunday evening in Mullanpur, there was a flash of something that had been absent from India's pace attack for a while — genuine menace from a tall, fast bowler who could make the ball do things that the batsman simply could not play.

It was Krishna's first Test wicket in India. That fact alone tells a story.

The 30-year-old Karnataka quick had played Tests overseas — in South Africa, in England — but his home opportunities had been scarce. Injuries, the depth of India's pace stocks, and the reality that Indian conditions rarely demand four seamers had kept him on the fringes. When India named their squad for the one-off Afghanistan Test, Krishna's inclusion felt like a nod to workload management as much as selection faith.

The Bowling

He proved otherwise. Bowling from the Pavilion End after India declared on 564 for eight, Krishna found immediate rhythm on a surface that was beginning to show its age. His first spell was sharp: back of a length, hitting the corridor outside off stump, and extracting just enough lateral movement to keep the Afghan batsmen guessing.

The Atal dismissal was textbook. Krishna angled the ball into the right-hander from wide of the crease, got it to straighten off the pitch, and breached the gap between bat and pad. Middle stump was uprooted. The speed gun read 140 kilometres per hour. More importantly, the control was immaculate — the kind of bowling that makes a captain trust a seamer in conditions that do not obviously suit him.

Then came the bigger scalp. Hashmatullah Shahidi, the Afghanistan captain, had looked the most composed of the visiting batsmen. He and Rahmat Shah had built a partnership of 76 runs that threatened to take the match into a different phase. Krishna ended it with a delivery that held its line outside off, drew Shahidi into a push, and took the edge. The ball carried comfortably to the slips.

Two wickets for 28 runs from 9 overs. Not explosive figures, but precisely the kind of bowling that complemented debutant Manav Suthar's left-arm spin at the other end. While Suthar turned and bounced and bamboozled, Krishna ensured that the batsmen could not simply survive against spin and cash in against pace.

The Context

India's pace rotation has been a talking point since the end of the Border-Gavaskar Trophy. Jasprit Bumrah is being managed for the Asian Games T20 squad and was not considered for this Test. Mohammed Siraj, who played as the senior seamer, bowled with heart but without the same incision. In that context, Krishna's performance was a quiet but significant statement of availability.

He is not a replacement for Bumrah — nobody is. But he offers something that India's other seamers do not always provide: genuine height that makes even good-length deliveries awkward, the ability to hit the seam consistently, and a bouncer that climbs uncomfortably on any surface.

For NRI fans who watched India's pace attack struggle for penetration in the home leg of the WTC cycle, Krishna's display was a reminder that India's bench strength in fast bowling is deeper than the playing elevens often suggest.

What It Means for Day 3

Afghanistan ended Day 2 at 113 for five, trailing by 451 runs. Rahmat Shah is the last recognised barrier, batting on 43 with quiet determination. If India can remove him early on Monday, the match could be wrapped up well before tea.

Krishna will be central to that effort. The Mullanpur pitch is offering enough for both pace and spin, and the morning session — when the ball traditionally does more under overcast conditions in the Punjab — should suit his method perfectly.

Three years is a long time to wait for a home Test opportunity. On this evidence, Prasidh Krishna should not have to wait that long again.
